title: Secure Quantum Metasurfaces for Direct Quantum Key Distribution Measurements
abstract: Quantum key distribution (QKD) can deliver information-theoretic security, but its receivers are still typically assembled from cascaded bulk optics. Metasurfaces offer a radical reduction in this complexity. Here, we make the metasurface function as the QKD measurement device itself. We design wavelength-specific dielectric apertures at 780, 1550, 2000, and 10 600 nm that interweave the linear H/V and circular R/L phase libraries at a 0.44--0.49λ cell pitch, i.e., below half the operating wavelength, and map the complete passive-BB84 measurement directly onto four detector channels. This subwavelength basis co-location prevents an ordinary propagating-wave aperture mask from isolating one basis without simultaneously attenuating or perturbing the other. Simulated full-wave focal-plane intensities are converted directly into conditional Born probabilities using fitted, calibration-fixed detector regions. The selected designs achieve probability fidelities of 97.96--99.08%, four-port collected efficiencies of 17.43--40.94%, and mean intrinsic quantum bit error rates of 1.42--3.96%. At 1550 nm, the selected design gives an asymptotic device-level yield of 0.151 secret bits per incident photon under an ideal single-photon model. Six-state detector tomography gives positive both-basis security bounds for all six reconstructed receiver models, including their polarization-dependent loss, basis imbalance and crosstalk. These results establish protocol-matched meta-optics as a route to compact, passive QKD receivers.
summary: This paper introduces the use of dielectric metasurfaces as integrated, passive measurement devices for Quantum Key Distribution (QKD). By engineering subwavelength apertures, the metasurface directly performs the necessary polarization and basis measurements for protocols like BB84. The results demonstrate high performance metrics, establishing a viable, compact, and scalable meta-optics route for next-generation quantum communication hardware.
main_problem: The primary challenge is developing a compact, passive measurement device capable of realizing the Positive-Operator-Valued Measure (POVM) required for Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) protocols like BB84, circumventing the complexity of traditional bulk optics.
main_result: The authors successfully demonstrated that protocol-matched meta-optics can function as the entire measurement device, achieving high fidelity (up to 99.08%) and a significant device-level secret key yield (0.151 bits/photon at 1550 nm).
method: The study uses full-wave simulations to design dielectric metasurfaces with subwavelength apertures that interweave polarization-dependent phase libraries, mapping the entire passive-BB84 measurement onto four detector channels.
model_or_system: The physical system is a dielectric metasurface fabricated with wavelength-specific apertures (e.g., at 780 nm, 1550 nm, 2000 nm, 10.6 $\mu$m). These structures are designed to perform the required polarization and basis measurements directly at the focal plane.
key_observables: Probability fidelities (97.96–99.08%), four-port collected efficiencies (17.43–40.94%), mean intrinsic QBER (1.42–3.96%), and asymptotic device-level secret key yield (e.g., 0.151 bits/photon at 1550 nm).
important_parameters: Operating wavelengths (780 nm, 1550 nm, 2000 nm, 10.6 $\mu$m); subwavelength cell pitch (0.44–0.49$\lambda$); and the specific polarization bases (H/V, R/L).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that detector regions are determined independently using fixed calibration methods to prevent post-processing bias, and the designs are treated as distinct for different operating wavelengths.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the focal-plane reconstruction of the BB84 measurement, showing interleaved sublattices and conditional responses. Supporting figures detail the characterization of various materials (Si, TiO2) and the extraction of Gaussian-fit parameters for detector response matrices.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the need for compact QKD measurement devices, detailing the metasurface design principles (subwavelength interleaving), presenting quantitative performance metrics across multiple wavelengths, and concluding with detailed characterization of the optical response using simulation and calibration diagnostics.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant to quantum optics and open quantum systems because it proposes a solid-state, integrated platform to perform fundamental quantum measurements (like those in QKD) with unprecedented compactness and efficiency, moving quantum technology from bulky lab setups to chip-scale devices.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Focal-plane reconstruction of the BB84 measurement. (a) Interleaved linear- and circular- basis sublattices. (b) Selected 1550 nm H-input far field with the calibration-fixed four-region integration boundaries. (c) Conditional response obtained from the integrated detector powers, with a probability fidelity of 99.08%. (d) Analysis sequence from the unit-cell sweep to the BB84 metrics. Each port centre is obtained from a local elliptical-Gaussian-plus-constant fit to its matched-state spot. One common square per device is the smallest that retains at least 99% of every fitted core and 95% of the empirical background- corrected energy, with no more than 10% fitted-baseline...

FIG. 2. Full-wave focal-plane intensity for the selected four-port designs. Rows show independent metasurfaces optimized at 780, 1550, 2000, and 10 600 nm; columns show H, V , R, and L inputs. Intensities are normalized within each panel for spatial comparison, while absolute transmission and collection are retained separately in the quantitative analysis. Rectangles show the calibration-fixed detector regions used in Equation (3).

FIG. 3. Conditional four-outcome response matrices. (a) Ideal passive BB84 response. (b–e) Responses calculated from the selected full-wave intensities at 780, 1550, 2000, and 10 600 nm, respectively, with probability fidelities of 0.980, 0.991, 0.983, and 0.989. Rows are input states and columns are detector outcomes in the order H, V, R, L; every row sums to unity over the four accepted regions. Diagonal entries are matched outcomes, the orthogonal port in the same basis represents a bit error, and the two outcomes in the conjugate basis form the ideally balanced random split.

FIG. 4. Optical and protocol metrics for the selected designs. (a) Basis-conditioned QBER. (b) Conditional probability fidelity. (c) Mean transmission, four-region focal-plane collection fraction, and collected efficiency. (d) Secret fraction after sifting and secret bits per incident photon under the asymptotic model in Equation (7).

FIG. 5. Effect of additional bit errors on secret-key yield. The curves show how the number of secret bits per incident photon decreases as additional errors are introduced into each device’s simulated measurement outcomes. The added errors flip a bit from 0 to 1 or from 1 to 0 with equal probability.
